The House of Representatives is considering a bill seeking to make the denial of conjugal rights for at least three months an additional ground for divorce in the country. The proposed amendment to the Matrimonial Causes Act, 2004, also seeks to recognise threats or infliction of grievous bodily harm, as well as emotional and psychological trauma, as grounds for seeking the dissolution of a marriage. The bill, sponsored by the member representing Aguata Federal Constituency of Anambra State, Dominic Okafor, seeks to expand the circumstances under which a spouse can obtain matrimonial relief under Section 16 of the principal Act. Titled “A Bill for an Act to Amend the Matrimonial Causes Act (MCA), Cap M7, Laws of the Federation of Nigeria, 2004, and for Matters Related Thereto,” the proposal was read for the first time on the floor of the House on Tuesday. It is expected to proceed to a second reading, where lawmakers will debate its general principles before further legislative consideration. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. Add us to your Preferred Sources Under one of the proposed provisions, a spouse who has “habitually and constantly denied or deprived” the petitioner of conjugal rights for a period of not less than three months could face divorce proceedings. The bill also proposes that a respondent who, since the celebration of the marriage, has “inflicted or threatens to inflict grievous bodily harm” on the petitioner should be recognised as a ground for matrimonial relief. Another provision seeks to recognise emotional and psychological trauma, allowing a petitioner to seek relief where the respondent has caused or continues to cause such trauma. However, the bill does not specify the evidentiary threshold courts would apply in determining claims of emotional and psychological trauma or prolonged denial of conjugal rights. The Matrimonial Causes Act is Nigeria’s principal legislation governing divorce and other matrimonial proceedings. Under the existing law, a marriage may be dissolved where the court is satisfied that it has broken down irretrievably. Among the grounds already recognised are wilful and persistent refusal to consummate a marriage, adultery, unreasonable behaviour, desertion, and prolonged separation. The Act also provides for divorce where a respondent has, for at least two years, been a habitual drunkard or habitually intoxicated through excessive use of sedative, narcotic, or stimulating drugs. It further recognises rape, sodomy, or bestiality committed by a respondent since the marriage as grounds for seeking dissolution. If passed by the National Assembly and assented to by the President, the proposed amendment would add the three new provisions to the legal framework governing divorce in Nigeria.
